This is also likely to be innate, as 8 day old boys showed more persistence/obsession/stubbornness in a study that put the babies in boxes, tied a string to their wrists which worked a mechanism to open a window to see their mothers' faces, and then after teaching them how to work the mechanism, disconnected it. Like in the interviewing.io data, the girls simply gave up/stopped wasting effort on pulling the string much earlier than the boys did.

So because early games were forced by technical limitations to rely heavily on raw difficulty for most/all of their depth and replayability, a "gamer" subculture grew around the medium that was not just male, but moreover the most obsessed males. As the medium developed and games became easier and could provide depth and replayability by other means, girls wanted in and were surprised to find the medium to be so thoroughly male.

Of course, this animated short, while amazing and inspiring, does not represent reality. I'm ambivalent about this little 8 minute piece of art. On the one hand, it feels incongruous--a male version of Twilight's adolescent female fantasy of a thoroughly safe bad boy chaste vegetarian vampire--a woman who loves you so much she'll obsess over keeping you so much it overpowers your obsession, and moreover, loves you for yourself so much it can withstand your descent into a loser stereotype. Edward Cullen doesn't expect sex, and our heroine here doesn't seem require anything of her man either. I guess there's a vague allusion to an exhausting job at the beginning, but not much beyond that.

On the other hand, what's wrong with teaching our daughters more persistence? Why not encourage more feminine understanding of male pursuits and habits, and while we're at it, why not use gaming to do it? Maybe no man ever is loved so fiercely or unconditionally, but perhaps it's a perfectly fine ideal to strive for.
